# Preparations

Load the necessary libraries

```{r}
#| label: libraries
#| output: false

#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| cache: false

library(tidyverse)  #for data wrangling etc
library(cmdstanr)   #for cmdstan
library(brms)       #for fitting models in STAN
library(standist)   #for exploring distributions
library(HDInterval) #for HPD intervals
library(posterior)  #for posterior draws
library(coda)       #for diagnostics
library(bayesplot)  #for diagnostics
library(rstan)      #for interfacing with STAN
library(DHARMa)     #for residual diagnostics
library(emmeans)    #for marginal means etc

source('helperFunctions.R')
```

# Scenario

A plant pathologist wanted to examine the effects of two different
strengths of tobacco virus on the number of lesions on tobacco leaves.
She knew from pilot studies that leaves were inherently very variable
in response to the virus. In an attempt to account for this leaf to
leaf variability, both treatments were applied to each leaf. Eight
individual leaves were divided in half, with half of each leaf
inoculated with weak strength virus and the other half inoculated with
strong virus. So the leaves were blocks and each treatment was
represented once in each block. A completely randomised design would
have had 16 leaves, with 8 whole leaves randomly allocated to each
treatment.

![Tobacco plant](../resources/TobaccoPlant.jpg){#fig-tobacco height="300"}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

LEAF   TREAT    NUMBER
------ -------- --------
1      Strong   35.898
1      Weak     25.02
2      Strong   34.118
2      Weak     23.167
3      Strong   35.702
3      Weak     24.122
\...   \...     \...

: Format of tobacco.csv data files {#tbl-tobacco .table-condensed}

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

------------ ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
**LEAF**     The blocking factor - Factor B
**TREAT**    Categorical representation of the strength of the tobacco virus - main factor of interest Factor A
**NUMBER**   Number of lesions on that part of the tobacco leaf - response variable
------------ ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

: Description of the variables in the tobacco data file {#tbl-tobacco1 .table-condensed}

:::
::::


# Read in the data

```{r}
#| label: readData
tobacco <- read_csv("../data/tobacco.csv", trim_ws = TRUE)

head(tobacco)
#LEAF is random effect (random effect is always categorical)
#NUMBER is response
#TREATMENT is fixed effect

tobacco <- tobacco |> 
  mutate(LEAF = factor(LEAF),
         TREATMENT = factor(TREATMENT))

#NUMBER is averaged so we are looking at a normal distribution
```



# Exploratory data analysis

```{r}
#| label: boxplot
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

tobacco |> ggplot(aes(y = NUMBER, x = TREATMENT)) +
  geom_boxplot() 

#normality = okay
#variance = okay
```

```{r}
#| label: pick-up-sticks plot
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

ggplot(tobacco, aes(y = NUMBER, x = TREATMENT, group = LEAF)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(aes(x = as.numeric(TREATMENT))) #can only draw lines between numbers

```

```{r}
#| label: model formula
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#ONLY bother fitting a random slopes if TREATMENT is within the block and if there are different slopes visible in above graph

tobacco_form <- bf(NUMBER ~ (1|LEAF) + TREATMENT, #1 = intercept and | = conditional on (Intercept is conditional on the LEAF)
              family = gaussian()
              )

```

```{r}
#| label: priors
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

get_prior(tobacco_form, data = tobacco)
#need priors for b, intercept (average of individual intercepts for first level of TREATMENT), sigma, and sd (variation in individual LEAF intercepts)

tobacco |> 
  group_by(TREATMENT) |> 
  summarise(median(NUMBER), mad(NUMBER))

priors <- prior(normal(35, 2.7), class = 'Intercept') + #for SD just round the first one
  prior(normal(0, 10), class = 'b') + #need to account for differences between medians so maybe go with 10
  prior(student_t(3, 0, 3.5), class='sigma') +
  prior(student_t(3, 0, 3.5), class='sd')
```

::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="50%"}

Random intercepts model formula:
$$
\begin{align}
y_{i,j} &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(\mu_{i,j}, \sigma^2)\\
\mu_{i,j} &=\beta_0 + \bf{Z_j}\boldsymbol{\gamma_j} + \bf{X_i}\boldsymbol{\beta} \\
\beta_0 &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(35, 3)\\
\beta_1 &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(0, 10)\\
\boldsymbol{\gamma_j} &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_l)\\
\sigma^2_l &\sim{} t(3, 0, 5)\\
\sigma^2 &\sim{} t(3, 0, 5)\
\end{align}
$$
::::
:::: {.column width="50%"}

Random intercept/slope model formula:
$$
\begin{align}
y_{i,j} &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(\mu_{i,j}, \sigma^2)\\
\mu_{i,j} &=\beta_0 + \bf{Z_j}\boldsymbol{\gamma_j} + \bf{X_i}\boldsymbol{\beta} \\
\beta_0 &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(35, 3)\\
\beta_1 &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(0, 10)\\
\boldsymbol{\gamma_j} &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(0, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})\\
\boldsymbol{\Sigma} &= \boldsymbol{D}({\sigma_l})\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{D}({\sigma_l^2})\\
\boldsymbol{\Omega} &\sim{} LKJ(\zeta)\\
\sigma_l^2 &\sim{} \mathcal{t}(3,0,5)\\
\sigma^2 &\sim{} \mathcal{t}(3, 0, 5)\
\end{align}
$$
::::
:::


where:

- $\bf{X}$ is the model matrix representing the overall intercept and
  effects of the treatment on the number of lesions.
- $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is a vector of the population-level effects
  parameters to be estimated.
- $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ is a vector of the group-level effect parameters
- $\bf{Z}$ represents a cell means model matrix for the random intercepts (and
  possibly random slopes) associated with leaves.
- the population-level intercept ($\beta_0$) has a gaussian prior with location
  of 31 and scale of 10
- the population-level effect ($\beta_1$) has a gaussian prior with location of
  0 and scale of 10
- the group-level effects are assumed to sum-to-zero and be drawn from a
  gaussian distribution with mean of 0 and covariance of $\Sigma$
- $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is the variance-covariance matrix between the
  groups (individual leaves).  It turns out that it is difficult to
  apply a prior on this covariance matrix, so instead, the covariance
  matrix is decomposed into a correlation matrix
  ($\boldsymbol{\Omega}$) and a vector of variances
  ($\boldsymbol{\sigma_l^2}$) which are the diagonals ($\boldsymbol{D}$)
  of the covariance matrix.
- $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$

$$
\begin{align}
\gamma &\sim{} N(0,\Sigma)\\
\Sigma &-> \Omega, \tau\\
\end{align}
$$

where $\Sigma$ is a covariance matrix.

# Fit the model

```{r}
#| label: fit model - priors only
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| cache: true

tobacco_brm2 <- brm(tobacco_form,
                 data = tobacco,
                 prior = priors,
                 sample_prior = 'only',
                 iter = 5000,
                 warmup = 1000,
                 chains = 3, cores = 3,
                 thin = 5,
                 refresh = 0,
                 backend = "cmdstanr",
                 seed = 1)

```

```{r}
#| label: conditional effect plot
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

tobacco_brm2 |> 
  conditional_effects() |> 
  plot(points = TRUE, ask = FALSE, plot = FALSE) |> 
  wrap_plots() &
  scale_y_log10()

#the priors must be very wide
```

```{r}
#| label: model with priors and data
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

tobacco_brm3 <- update(tobacco_brm2, sample_prior = 'yes', refresh = 0)

#random effects usually cause sharp features in the posterior and makes divergent transitions (divergence)
#BUT you can control for this by telling the model to learn more thoroughly the physics of the posterior

tobacco_brm3 <- update(tobacco_brm2,
                       sample_prior = 'yes',
                       control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99),
                       refresh = 0)

tobacco_brm3 |> 
  conditional_effects() |> 
  plot(points = TRUE, ask = FALSE, plot = FALSE) |> 
  wrap_plots() &
  scale_y_log10()

#priors are clearly not driving the posterior
```

# MCMC sampling diagnostics

```{r}
#| label: examine all priors and posteriors
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

tobacco_brm3 |> 
  SUYR_prior_and_posterior()

```

# Partial effects plots

```{r}
#| label: model diagnostics
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

tobacco_brm3$fit |> stan_trace(inc_warmup = TRUE)

tobacco_brm3$fit |> stan_ac() #pay the most attention to sigma

tobacco_brm3$fit |> stan_rhat()

tobacco_brm3$fit |> stan_ess()
```

```{r}
#| label: posterior probs density overlay
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

tobacco_brm3 |> pp_check(type = 'dens_overlay', ndraws=100)

#dark line is actual distribution of our data
```

```{r}
#| label: simulate residuals
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

tobacco.resids <- make_brms_dharma_res(tobacco_brm3, integerResponse = TRUE)
testUniformity(tobacco.resids)
plotResiduals(tobacco.resids, quantreg = FALSE) #because there are so few points we add FALSE
testDispersion(tobacco.resids)
```

# Model investigation

```{r}
#| label: summary table
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#absolute scale
tobacco_brm3 |> 
  as_draws_df() |> 
  dplyr::select(matches("^b_.*|^sigma$|^sd_.*")) |> 
  summarise_draws(median, 
                  HDInterval::hdi,
                  rhat, 
                  ess_bulk,
                  Pl = ~mean(.x < 0), #less than 
                  Pg = ~mean(.x > 0)) #greater than

#Intercept: Average number of lesions in the strong treatment was 36.
#Weak lesion has 8 less lesions (strong evidence).
#sigma = unexplained variance (4.2 units of variation)
#sd is how variable the different leaves are (3 units)

#TREATMENT and LEAF scale have similar levels of variance (sd_LEAF vs sigma)
```

```{r}
#| label: fractional scale table
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#transformed to logs, substracted the two, and then back transformed to get a percentage difference
tobacco_brm3 |> 
  emmeans(~TREATMENT) |> 
  regrid(transform = "log") |> 
  pairs() |> 
  regrid()

#The strong treatment produces 27% more lesions than the weak treatment.

```


```{r}
#| label: R2
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

tobacco_brm3 |> 
  bayes_R2(re.form = NA, summary=FALSE) |> 
  median_hdci()
#y = R^2, 37% of variation in lesions can be explained by treatment (fixed effects only)

#conditional R2 - variation explained by fixed and random effects
tobacco_brm3 |> 
  bayes_R2(re.form = ~(1|LEAF), summary=FALSE) |> 
  median_hdci()
#y = R^2, 60% of variation in lesions can be explained by treatment (fixed effects AND random effects) --> total amount explained

#40% of variation unexplained
```

# Further investigations
## Fit the random intercept and random slope model

```{r}
#| label: random intercept and slope formula
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#1 represents intercept, would usually be (1 + TREATMENT|LEAF)
#TREATMENT|LEAF is a slope for TREATMENT
#its saying intercept and slope are conditional on LEAF (because in the plot we saw different slopes and intercepts for different leaves)
tobacco_form <- bf(NUMBER ~ (TREATMENT|LEAF) + TREATMENT, 
                   family = gaussian())

```

```{r}
#| label: get priors
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

get_prior(tobacco_form, data = tobacco)
#need a new prior for "cor" --> correlation between intercept and slope
#but its very simple, the default prior is the only sensible prior (lkj(1))

priors <- priors +
  prior(lkj_corr_cholesky(1), class='cor')

```

```{r}
#| label: model with priors and data 2
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

tobacco_random <- brm(tobacco_form,
                 data = tobacco,
                 prior = priors,
                 sample_prior = 'yes',
                 iter = 5000,
                 warmup = 1600,
                 chains = 3, cores = 3,
                 thin = 5,
                 refresh = 0,
                 backend = "cmdstanr",
                 seed = 1,
                 control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99))

#if you get divergence even after adjusting the delta, then increase warmup
#want divergent transitions < 10

```
# MCMC sampling diagnostics

```{r}
#| label: examine all priors and posteriors 2
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

tobacco_random |> 
  SUYR_prior_and_posterior()

#we aren't interested in correlation so its not a problem that the prior and posterior are so similar
```

```{r}
#| label: conditional effects plot 2
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

tobacco_random |> 
  conditional_effects() |> 
  plot(points = TRUE)

```

```{r}
#| label: model diagnostics again
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

tobacco_random$fit |> stan_trace(inc_warmup = TRUE)

tobacco_random$fit |> stan_ac()

tobacco_random$fit |> stan_rhat()

tobacco_random$fit |> stan_ess() #ESS is low

tobacco_random |> pp_check(type = 'dens_overlay', ndraws=100)
```

```{r}
#| label: simulate residuals again
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

tobacco.resids <- make_brms_dharma_res(tobacco_random, integerResponse = TRUE)
testUniformity(tobacco.resids)
plotResiduals(tobacco.resids, quantreg = FALSE)
testDispersion(tobacco.resids)

```

```{r}
#| label: summary table 2
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#absolute scale
tobacco_random |> 
  as_draws_df() |> 
  dplyr::select(matches("^b_.*|^sigma$|^sd_.*")) |> 
  summarise_draws(median, 
                  HDInterval::hdi,
                  rhat, 
                  ess_bulk,
                  Pl = ~mean(.x < 0), #less than 
                  Pg = ~mean(.x > 0)) #greater than

#Intercept: Average number of lesions in the strong treatment was 36.
#Weak lesion has 8 less lesions (strong evidence).
#sigma = unexplained variance (3.9 units of variation)
#sd_LEAF__Intercept is how variable the different leaves are (3 units)
#sd_LEAF__TREATMENTWeak is how variable the treatment is for different leaves (2 units) --> went down comapred to the random intercept model

```

```{r}
#| label: comapre models
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

loo_compare(loo(tobacco_brm3), loo(tobacco_random)) 
#not different from each other when you add se_diff to elpd_diff so wasn't worth the extra effort to fit a random slope and intercept model
```

```{r}
#| label: R2 again
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

tobacco_random |> 
  bayes_R2(re.form = NA, summary=FALSE) |> 
  median_hdci()
#y = R^2, 35% of variation in lesions can be explained by treatment (fixed effects only)

#conditional R2 - variation explained by fixed and random effects
tobacco_random |> 
  bayes_R2(re.form = ~TREATMENT|LEAF, summary=FALSE) |> 
  median_hdci()
#y = R^2, 66% of variation in lesions can be explained by treatment (fixed effects AND random effects) --> total amount explained

#34% of variation unexplained
```
